conventional_description:
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a progressive lung condition characterized by persistent airflow limitation. It's usually caused by long-term exposure to irritants-most commonly cigarette smoke-that damage the airways and air sacs. The main symptoms are shortness of breath, a chronic cough, and excess mucus production.
Doctors diagnose COPD using spirometry, which measures how much air you can exhale and how fast. The disease is typically classified into stages (mild to very severe) based on lung function. While treatments can relieve symptoms and slow progression, the damage to the lungs is considered irreversible.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management of COPD centers on bronchodilators (inhaled medications that relax airway muscles) and corticosteroids to reduce inflammation. For acute exacerbations, oral steroids and antibiotics may be used. Pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen therapy for advanced stages, and smoking cessation are also cornerstones of care. In select cases, surgical options like lung volume reduction or transplant are considered.
tcm_understanding:
TCM views COPD as a disorder of the Lungs, but the root often lies in the Spleen and Kidneys. The Lung governs Qi and breath; when weakened by chronic illness or external pathogens, it fails to descend and diffuse Qi, causing cough and breathlessness. Over time, a weak Spleen fails to transform fluids, producing phlegm that clogs the airways. A deficient Kidney cannot 'grasp' the Qi, making inhalation shallow and labored.
Phlegm is the key pathological factor-it's not just mucus but a thick, turbid substance that obstructs the Lungs. Depending on the underlying imbalance, phlegm can be cold and watery, hot and sticky, or damp and profuse. This explains why COPD symptoms vary so much between individuals: one person may cough up copious white froth, while another struggles with thick yellow plugs.
TCM distinguishes between the root (deficiency) and the branch (excess). In stable COPD, the root deficiency of Qi or Yang dominates-manifesting as fatigue, cold limbs, or a weak voice. During an exacerbation, excess factors like Phlegm-Heat or Damp-Phlegm flare up. Effective treatment must address both layers simultaneously, clearing the phlegm without further weakening the body.
That's why one Western diagnosis maps to multiple TCM patterns. The pattern is determined by the nature of the cough, sputum, breathlessness, and accompanying signs like cold intolerance or poor appetite. The tongue and pulse provide the final confirmation. This personalized approach aims not just to open the airways but to correct the underlying imbalances that generate phlegm and weakness in the first place.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening to the cough and asking about the sputum - its color, consistency, and quantity. This is the first big clue, because each pattern produces a very different kind of phlegm. The quality of the breathlessness and what makes it better or worse also steer the diagnosis toward either a primarily excess (phlegm) or a primarily deficiency (weakness) picture.
If the sputum is copious, sticky, and white - like uncooked egg white - and the chest feels tight and heavy, the pattern is likely Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs. The tongue typically has a thick, greasy white coating and the pulse feels slippery, like pearls rolling on a plate. This picture points to the Spleen failing to manage fluids.
When the person is more fatigued than tight, with a weak cough, pale complexion, and only a little thin, watery phlegm, the root is Spleen and Lung Qi Deficiency. The tongue is pale and slightly puffy, and the pulse is weak and forceless. The shortness of breath is constant, not just during a flare-up, and eating or exertion makes it worse.
During an acute flare, the phlegm can turn yellow, thick, and hard to cough up, accompanied by a feeling of heat and oppression in the chest. This shift signals Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs. The tongue becomes red with a sticky yellow coat, and the pulse turns rapid and slippery. Fever or a general sense of warmth may appear.
In advanced COPD, the practitioner listens for where the breath gets stuck. If the struggle is mainly on the inhale - as if the body cannot pull air deep into the lower belly - the pattern is Kidneys failing to receive Qi. The pulse is deep and weak, especially at the rear position, and the person often looks drawn and exhausted.
When cold intolerance, a pale face, and a deep, slow pulse accompany the chronic cough, Lung and Kidney Yang Deficiency is the root. The fire that warms the body and moves Qi has dimmed. The tongue is pale and wet, and the breathlessness is worse in cold weather or after any chill.
If swelling appears in the ankles or face and urination becomes scanty, the pattern has progressed to Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing. The tongue is pale and swollen with a wet coating. This water retention further crowds the Lungs, making every breath a labor.
The most serious warning sign is a change in mental state. When a person with COPD becomes confused, drowsy, or restless, with a loud rattling cough and a thick, greasy white tongue coat, Phlegm Misting the Heart is present. This is an emergency that requires immediate medical attention.

patterns.symptoms: ["Cough with copious, white, sticky phlegm that is easy to expectorate", "Feeling of heaviness and fullness in the chest", "Poor appetite, bloating, and loose stools", "Fatigue and a sensation of heaviness in the body", "Nausea or a stuffy feeling in the upper abdomen"]
patterns.worse_with: Damp or humid environments, Dairy, greasy, or fried foods, Overeating or large meals, Cold and raw foods, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Warm, dry weather, Light, easily digestible meals, Gentle movement (walking, tai chi), Steam inhalation, Warm ginger or cardamom tea
patterns.why_this_happens: In COPD, the Spleen often becomes too weak to transform fluids properly, turning them into a sticky, turbid substance called Damp-Phlegm. This phlegm rises up and settles in the Lungs, clogging the airways like a thick sludge. The result is the hallmark chest tightness, a heavy cough, and copious white phlegm that is relatively easy to bring up because the dampness makes it loose rather than dry and stuck.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and swollen with teeth marks, covered by a thick, white, greasy coating that looks wet. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá), like beads rolling under the fingers, especially noticeable at the Lung (right cun) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs is rooted in a weak Spleen that fails to transform fluids. Cold, raw, and greasy foods further damage the Spleen and add more dampness, while humid environments make the body's internal dampness heavier. Warmth, light meals, and gentle movement all strengthen the Spleen and help Qi move, which dries up dampness and clears the phlegm. Steam inhalation directly moistens and loosens the sticky phlegm so the Lungs can expel it more easily.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods, as well as dairy, which all promote dampness and phlegm. Focus on warm, cooked meals like soups and stews with gentle spices (ginger, cardamom) to support the Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi flow and keeps the Lungs clear, while steam inhalation can loosen phlegm.

patterns.symptoms: ["Chronic weak cough with thin watery phlegm", "Shortness of breath that worsens on exertion", "Poor appetite and abdominal bloating", "Fatigue and general weakness", "Pale face without lustre", "Spontaneous sweating and catching colds easily"]

patterns.better_with: Rest and avoiding overexertion, Warm, cooked meals, Gentle breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it cannot transform food and fluids into usable Qi, so dampness and phlegm build up. The Lung depends on Spleen Qi to stay strong; without it, Lung Qi becomes too weak to descend and diffuse. This leaves you with a chronic weak cough, thin watery phlegm, and that constant, exhausting shortness of breath that worsens with any effort.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a thin white slippery coating. Pulse: weak and forceless overall, especially deficient at the right cun (Lung) and guan (Spleen) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overexertion further depletes Qi, while rest allows it to recover. Raw and cold foods impair Spleen function, worsening phlegm production, whereas warm cooked foods are easy to digest and support Qi. Protecting against wind and cold prevents external pathogens from further weakening the Lung's defensive Qi.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Gentle breathing exercises and tai chi can support Lung Qi without overexertion. Rest adequately and protect against wind and cold.

patterns.symptoms: ["Thick yellow or green sputum", "Chest oppression with a feeling of heat", "Thirst and flushed face", "Wheezing with gurgling sounds in the throat", "Restlessness and irritability"]

patterns.better_with: Cool fresh air, Steam inhalation, Light, non-greasy meals, Rest and calm
patterns.why_this_happens: In COPD, long-standing Damp-Phlegm can stagnate and generate Heat, or an external Wind-Heat pathogen can trigger a flare-up. This Heat fuses with the Phlegm to form a sticky, obstructive mixture that clogs the airways. The result is the classic exacerbation picture of thick yellow sputum, chest oppression, and labored breathing.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen at the front, with a yellow greasy coating and maybe red prickles on the front third. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò), strongest at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs is fueled by warmth and dampness, so cooling, light, and moistening measures help clear the Heat and loosen the Phlegm. Spicy, greasy foods and smoking generate more Heat and sticky Phlegm, directly aggravating the obstruction. Rest conserves Qi and prevents the body from generating excess Heat, while steam and fresh air help the Lungs expel the thick phlegm.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods that generate phlegm and heat. Eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, radish, and watercress. Drink plenty of warm water and use steam inhalation to loosen sticky phlegm. Stay away from smoke and polluted air, and keep the room air fresh and slightly cool.

patterns.symptoms: ["Inhalation feels short and insufficient; exhalation is easier", "Chronic breathlessness that worsens with even light exertion", "Lower back soreness and weak knees", "Fatigue, low motivation, and a quiet, weak voice", "Spontaneous sweating with activity"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion or too much walking, Cold weather or drafts, Emotional stress and anxiety, Large, heavy meals, Lying completely flat
patterns.better_with: Rest and avoiding overexertion, Warmth, especially on the lower back, Gentle, slow breathing exercises, Small, warm meals, Humidified air
patterns.why_this_happens: In advanced COPD, the Kidneys lose their ability to grasp Qi and pull it down into the body. Instead of sinking to the lower abdomen, the breath gets stuck in the chest, making inhalation feel short and labored while exhalation is easier. This deep-rooted deficiency also weakens the lower back and knees, drains stamina, and leaves you winded after even mild activity.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with teeth marks and a thin white moist coating. Pulse: deep and weak, especially feeble at the rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overexertion drains the already depleted Kidney Qi, making it even harder for the Kidneys to grasp the breath. Cold constricts and further weakens Kidney Yang, while stress causes Qi to rise and scatter. Rest, warmth, and gentle breathing help conserve and direct Qi downward, supporting the Kidneys' role in anchoring the breath.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep warm, especially the lower back and feet, and avoid cold drafts. Gentle breathing exercises, like pursed-lip breathing, can help train the breath to sink. Eat small, warm, easily digested meals and avoid raw or icy foods that chill the body.

patterns.symptoms: ["Feeling cold all over, especially back and limbs", "Thin, watery or frothy sputum", "Lower back and knee soreness and weakness", "Frequent urination, especially at night", "Shortness of breath that worsens with the slightest movement", "Profound fatigue and lack of stamina"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold weather or drafts, Overexertion, Eating cold or raw foods, Emotional stress, Exposure to cold
patterns.better_with: Warm drinks and soups, Moxibustion on the lower back, Gentle breathing exercises, Rest and staying warm, Ginger and cinnamon in food
patterns.why_this_happens: In COPD, the Lungs and Kidneys work together to manage breathing and fluids. When their Yang energy is depleted, the body loses its internal warmth. This leads to cold-phlegm accumulating in the airways, causing a chronic cough with thin, watery sputum. The Kidneys can no longer 'grasp' the Qi, so every breath feels shallow and exertion quickly brings on severe shortness of breath. The lack of warming Yang also causes cold limbs, a pale face, and deep fatigue.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender with tooth marks; white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, and slow; the right Cun (Lung) position feels especially empty, and both Chi (Kidney) positions are weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold depletes Yang further, so warmth is the most direct remedy. Warm foods and moxibustion gently restore the body's internal fire, helping to transform thin phlegm and ease breathing. Rest conserves the little Yang energy available, while overexertion scatters it. Stress tightens the chest and consumes Qi, making it harder for the weakened Lungs and Kidneys to function.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and include warming spices such as ginger, cinnamon, and a little black pepper. Avoid raw, cold, and iced foods and drinks, which further chill the body. Keep the chest, back, and feet warm, especially in cold weather. Gentle movement like tai chi and pursed-lip breathing exercises can help, but stop before you feel breathless. Moxibustion at home on the lower back can be deeply restorative.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney Yang Deficiency with Water overflowing
patterns.symptoms: ["Swelling of the legs and ankles", "Feeling of cold in the lower body", "Scanty or difficult urination", "Soreness and weakness of the lower back", "Breathlessness on exertion", "Cold hands and feet"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Overexertion, Excess salt or fluid intake, Raw, cold foods, Prolonged standing
patterns.better_with: Warmth (heating pad on lower back), Rest with legs elevated, Warm, cooked meals, Gentle movement, Moxibustion
patterns.why_this_happens: In advanced COPD, when Kidney Yang is severely depleted, the body's warming fire can no longer transform and move fluids. Water accumulates, first causing swelling in the legs and ankles. This excess fluid can overflow upward, congesting the lungs and making breathing even more labored. The deep internal cold leaves the whole body, especially the lower back and limbs, feeling chilled and weak.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, teeth-marked body with a white slippery coating and an excessively wet surface. Pulse: deep, slow, weak, especially faint at the proximal (Chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's warming fire. Cold and dampness extinguish this fire, worsening water retention and breathlessness. Warmth, rest, and moxibustion restore Yang, helping the body transform fluids. Elevating the legs uses gravity to drain edema, while gentle movement keeps Qi flowing without depleting energy. Salty and raw foods burden the Kidneys and Spleen, increasing water accumulation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked foods like soups and stews. Use warming spices such as ginger, cinnamon, and black pepper. Avoid cold, raw, and damp-producing foods (dairy, greasy foods). Keep the lower back and legs warm, and elevate the legs when sitting to help reduce swelling. Gentle movement like tai chi or walking supports Qi circulation, but avoid overexertion that depletes Yang.

patterns.symptoms: ["Mental confusion or dullness", "Rattling or gurgling sound in the throat", "Chest stuffiness and oppression", "Slurred or unclear speech"]
patterns.worse_with: Damp, cold weather, Greasy, heavy foods, Prolonged inactivity, Emotional withdrawal
patterns.better_with: Warm, dry environment, Light, easily digestible meals, Gentle movement and breathing exercises, Mental stimulation and companionship
patterns.why_this_happens: In advanced COPD, long-standing phlegm-dampness from a weakened Spleen and Lungs can become thick and turbid. This turbid phlegm rises along the channels to cloud the Heart's orifices, which house the mind. When the Heart's connection to the outside world is blocked, mental clarity fades, consciousness becomes muddled, and a rattling sound appears in the throat.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with a thick, white, greasy coating; may appear stiff or sluggish. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá), round and smooth, with good strength, most pronounced at the middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm is a Yin pathogen that thrives in cold and damp conditions, so warmth and dryness help the body dissolve it. Light, warm foods support the Spleen in transforming fluids properly, preventing new phlegm from forming. Gentle movement and breathing exercises keep Qi and phlegm moving, while mental engagement and social connection stimulate the Heart's orifices, counteracting the clouding effect of turbid phlegm.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the living environment warm and dry, and avoid damp, cold places. Eat small, warm, easily digested meals like rice congee with a little ginger; strictly avoid dairy, greasy foods, and raw cold items that create more phlegm. Gentle daily movement and deep breathing exercises help keep the chest open, while staying socially engaged and mentally active supports the Heart's clarity.

formulas.properties: Warm, Warms the Lungs and Transforms Phlegm-Fluids, Descends Qi, Stops Cough and Calms Wheezing
formulas.description: A gentle, three-herb formula made entirely from common plant seeds, originally created to help elderly parents suffering from chronic cough with heavy phlegm, chest congestion, and poor digestion. It works by dissolving accumulated phlegm in the chest, calming rebellious Qi that causes coughing and wheezing, and improving digestion to stop new phlegm from forming. Despite its simplicity, it remains one of the most widely used formulas for phlegm-related respiratory conditions.

It is used for people who experience poor appetite, bloating, loose stools, nausea, and fatigue due to a weakened digestive system that has allowed excess moisture and phlegm to build up in the body.

formulas.properties: Cool, Clears Heat and Transforms Phlegm, Regulates Qi and stops cough, Descends Lung Qi and Calms Wheezing
formulas.description: A classical formula for coughs with thick, sticky, yellow phlegm caused by Heat and Phlegm congesting the Lungs. It clears Heat, breaks down stubborn Phlegm, and restores the normal downward flow of Lung Qi to relieve coughing, chest fullness, and wheezing.

formulas.translation: Ginseng and Gecko Powder · Sòng dynasty, 1047 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Tonifies Lung and Kidney Qi, Stops Cough and Calms Wheezing, Clears Lung Heat
formulas.description: A classical formula for people with long-standing cough and wheezing caused by weakness of the Lungs and Kidneys, especially when accompanied by thick yellow phlegm, chest irritability, or coughing up blood-streaked sputum. It works by strengthening the body's deep respiratory capacity while clearing lingering Heat and dissolving phlegm.

formulas.translation: Golden Cabinet Kidney Qi Pill · Eastern Hàn dynasty, circa 200 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Tonifies Kidney Yang, Warms Yang and Transforms Qi, Warms the Ming Men Fire
formulas.description: A classical formula that gently warms and supports the Kidneys to restore vitality, fluid balance, and lower body warmth. It is used for people with Kidney weakness who experience lower back soreness, cold legs, frequent urination or difficulty urinating, and general fatigue. Unlike strong warming formulas, it uses a small amount of warming herbs alongside a larger base of nourishing ingredients, working gradually to restore the body's natural balance.

formulas.translation: True Warrior Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, circa 200 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Warms Yang and Disperses Cold, Promotes Urination and Drains Dampness, Transforms Water-Dampness
formulas.description: A classical formula for people who feel persistently cold, experience swelling or puffiness (especially in the legs), have reduced urine output, and may suffer from dizziness, loose stools, or palpitations. These symptoms arise when the body's warming energy is too weak to properly manage fluids, causing water to accumulate where it shouldn't. Zhen Wu Tang warms the body's core while gently helping it drain excess fluid through urination.

formulas.translation: Two-Aged Herb Decoction · Sòng dynasty, 1078–1148 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Dries Dampness and Transforms Phlegm, Regulates Qi and Harmonizes the Middle Burner, Directs Rebellious Qi Downward and Stops Vomiting
formulas.description: A foundational formula used to clear excess phlegm and dampness from the body, especially when they cause coughing with white phlegm, nausea, chest tightness, dizziness, or a heavy feeling in the limbs. It works by drying dampness, dissolving phlegm, and supporting healthy digestion. Named for its two key ingredients, Ban Xia and Chen Pi, which are most effective when aged.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help my breathing?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture can help relax the muscles around the airways, reduce inflammation, and calm the breath. Many patients notice that after a session, their chest feels less tight and they can breathe more deeply. Regular acupuncture also strengthens the body's overall Qi, which can reduce the frequency of flare-ups. Points like Feishu (BL-13) and Dingchuan (EX-B-1) are specifically used to open the lungs.

faqs.question: Will Chinese herbs interact with my COPD medications?
faqs.answer: In general, Chinese herbs are safe to take alongside inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. However, some herbs that move Blood or thin phlegm may theoretically interact with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your lung doctor about everything you're taking. If you use oral steroids during an exacerbation, your herbal formula may be adjusted to support your body while you taper off the medication.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM for COPD?
faqs.answer: Most people notice some improvement within 2-4 weeks-less phlegm, easier expectoration, and reduced chest tightness. Breathlessness often improves more gradually, especially if the root deficiency is deep. For chronic, long-standing COPD, treatment is typically ongoing, with the goal of reducing exacerbations and maintaining quality of life rather than a complete cure.

faqs.question: What should I eat to reduce phlegm?
faqs.answer: To prevent phlegm buildup, avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods as well as dairy and sugar, which are considered 'phlegm-producing' in TCM. Instead, favor warm, cooked meals like soups, stews, and congees. Pears (especially Asian pears) can moisten the Lungs, while almonds and walnuts support the Kidneys and help anchor the breath. Ginger tea can warm the Lungs and thin phlegm.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe during a COPD flare-up?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be very effective during a flare-up to clear phlegm and heat, but you should never rely on it as a substitute for emergency medical care. If you have severe breathlessness, blue lips, or confusion, seek urgent care immediately. For mild to moderate exacerbations, a TCM practitioner can adjust your herbal formula to address the acute symptoms while still supporting your underlying constitution.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse lung damage?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot reverse structural damage like destroyed air sacs, but it can significantly improve how the remaining lung tissue functions. By reducing phlegm, inflammation, and airway constriction, many people experience better oxygen exchange, less breathlessness, and a greater ability to carry out daily activities. The goal is to maximize your quality of life and slow disease progression.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
research.description: A 2019 Cochrane systematic review of 12 randomized controlled trials involving 796 participants found that acupuncture, when added to usual care, may improve quality of life and reduce breathlessness in people with COPD. The review noted that the evidence for lung function improvement was inconclusive and called for larger, well-designed studies.
research.periodical: Coyle ME, Shergis JL, Liu S, et al. Acupuncture for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2019, Issue 6. Art. No.: CD009439.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This 2018 meta-analysis of 28 RCTs with 2,643 participants evaluated Chinese herbal medicine as an add-on to conventional treatment. It found that herbal formulas significantly reduced exacerbation frequency, improved the six-minute walk distance, and enhanced quality of life compared to conventional treatment alone. The most frequently used herbs included Huang Qi, Dang Shen, and Bai Zhu, consistent with Spleen and Lung Qi Deficiency patterns.
research.periodical: Chen X, May BH, Di YM, et al. Oral Chinese herbal medicine combined with pharmacotherapy for stable COPD: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Complementary Therapies in Medicine. 2018;39:137-150.

research.title: Bu-Fei Jian-Pi granules for stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
research.description: A 2016 placebo-controlled RCT in 120 patients with stable COPD and Spleen-Lung Qi Deficiency pattern showed that Bu-Fei Jian-Pi granules significantly improved dyspnea scores and reduced the frequency of acute exacerbations over six months. The herbal group also showed better nutritional status and less fatigue, supporting the TCM principle of strengthening the Spleen to support the Lungs.
research.periodical: Li JS, Li SY, Yu XQ, et al. Bu-Fei Jian-Pi granules for stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Trials. 2016;17:219.
